------------------------------------------------------------ By Mags Corliss | Bay Tribune October came in with a breeze off the Bay and the sound of things actually happening. I have sat in this chair for eighty-nine editions watching initiatives pass council votes and then stall in implementation hallways. I have written headlines about programs approved, funding authorized, deadlines set — and then written the follow-ups about deadlines missed, funding frozen, and programs that existed on paper and nowhere else. This month is different. Not because the city suddenly became competent — it took an executive order, a public shaming, and a press conference that arrived twenty minutes too late to change the thing it was protesting. But the results are real. Chief Montez signed the OARI dispatch agreement. Crisis responders will take their first calls in Districts 1, 3, and 5. Beverly Hayes will receive $18,500 she was promised eight months ago. Foundation piles will go into the ground at the Baylight waterfront. Things moved. Not gracefully.

----- THE ATTORNEY Before he was the people’s mayor, Avery Santana was the people’s lawyer. He graduated from Berkeley Law in 2000 and went straight into civil rights litigation — housing discrimination, police misconduct, employment retaliation. He never chased the big corporate cases. He stayed in the neighborhoods, in the storefronts, in the community centers where people who couldn’t afford downtown firms came looking for help. “I had offers,” he said. “Good ones. San Francisco. Los Angeles. But I kept thinking about my father. He unloaded ships for three decades so I could have choices. What kind of choice would it be to leave the place that made me?” He built a reputation as a tenacious litigator — the kind of attorney who wouldn’t settle when settling meant his client got less than they deserved. He won a landmark housing case in 2011 that established new protections for tenants facing illegal evictions. He represented families after the 2009 BART shooting.

I’ve covered ballplayers for fifty years, and few ever mastered the invisible art — the sense that presence itself can change probability. Keane did. Every generation gets one like him — a reminder that the game, and the people who love it, are still worth saving.

Hal Richmond Part V — Darrin Davis and Oakland’s Left Field Bloodline Some positions in baseball get filled. Others get inherited. Left field in Oakland has always belonged to a particular kind of player — not defined by shape or speed or even skill, but by presence. The men who played the position best didn’t blend into the lineup. They bent the structure of innings. They shifted the temperature of the ballpark. They forced opposing pitchers to change the way they breathed between pitches. Rickey Henderson was the first to do it with certainty. Yoenis Céspedes did it with spectacle. Khris Davis did it with concentrated force. Darrin Davis does it with something else entirely — a volume of damage that arrives so regularly that people forget how uncommon his seasons actually are.
